newsitem.title: JORDAN: Hamas leader returns to Jordan "a free man".
newsitem.headline: Hamas leader returns to Jordan "a free man".

text.p: Musa Abu Marzook, political leader of the militant Palestinian movement Hamas, flew back to Jordan a free man after two years in a New York jail accused of "terrorist activity", Jordanian officials said on Tuesday.

Abu Marzook, expelled by Jordan in 1995 under pressure from Washington, Israel and the Palestinians and arrested shortly afterwards, returned to Jordan on board a special U.S. military plane which landed at Amman military airport late on Monday.
Jordan insisted it was putting no constraints on his activities but said he would be subject to Jordanian law. Diplomats said his movements would be closely monitored.
"He is a free man. He is not under our custody," Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawneh told reporters.

His deportation from the United States followed an Israeli decision to drop a demand for his extradition, despite allegations that he was involved in a wave of attacks against Israelis between 1990 and 1994.
Israel also said he raised money for and controlled the leadership of the military wing of Hamas, an Islamist movement which rejects the Palestinian self-rule deal with Israel as a sell-out.
Abu Marzook, who denied involvement in violence and said his activities in Jordan had been purely political, said in a statement issued in New York that Hamas could not be crushed.

"Hamas is a major voice of the Palestinian people whose rights have been ignored since the creation of Israel," he said. "To Israel and the Israelis I say that you can not make a false peace while usurping Palestinian rights."

Israeli security officials said in February that Israel, fearing a wave of violent protests if Abu Marzook were transferred to an Israeli jail, would drop the extradition request in return for a pledge to shun violence.
But Amman-based Hamas officials denied their leader was returning under pre-conditions and said he would resume a leading political role in the group once settled in Amman.
"We expect Dr Abu Marzook to continue his role in Hamas," the organisation's representative in Jordan Mohammad Nazzal told Reuters.
Abu Marzook's defence lawyer said in New York he denied "he has ever participated in terrorist activities or intends to ever participate in terrorist activities."

Jordan, which says its decision to admit Abu Marzook once again is purely a humanitarian decision, has been careful this time to make sure that it first received a written U.S. request to shelter him.
But it is anxious not to be seen to be putting Abu Marzook under house arrest on behalf of Washington or Israel.
"(Abu Marzook) will be dignified and living in Jordan to according to this (humanitarian) principle," Tarawneh said.
Diplomats said Abu Marzook, like other Hamas officials in Amman, would find his activities closely monitored.

"The public line is that he has not committed any crime. But in practice his movements will be subject to very close scrutiny," said one Western diplomat. "He will be told quite clearly not to engage in any activity which could be construed as terrorism."
Suicide bombers from the military wing of Hamas killed dozens of Israelis in a series of bomb attacks one year ago.
